awd_titl_txt: Conference: 2025 Society for Biological Engineering Conference Support for Future Leaders
awd_abstract_narration:
The primary goal of this project is to ensure that student trainees and early career professionals in the fields of synthetic biology, biotechnology and synthetic microbial systems are able to attend important conferences. This support is viewed as an investment in the biotechnology workforce of the future, providing trainees and early career professionals with an opportunities to share their work, develop relationships and advance their careers.  This support will apply to trainees and early career professionals working at U.S.-based universities, building a strong national pipeline to ensure the United States continues to be a leader in science and engineering disciplines.

The Society for Biological Engineering (SBE) organizes conferences to advance the industries, research areas and careers of biological engineers, and people working in related areas. The conferences focus on developing a high-quality technical program to share the latest technical developments, networking opportunities to build community and engaging trainees and early career professionals to build a strong future for the field. Four of its key conferences in synthetic biology are: Synthetic Biology: Engineering, Evolution and Design (SEED), Mammalian Synthetic Biology (mSBW), Cell Free Systems and the International Conference on Microbiome Engineering (ICME). It is important to engage the next generation of synthetic biologists in these meetings, to facilitate the transfer of knowledge and offer development opportunities. This project's goals are to help students and early career professionals attend conferences in the fields of synthetic biology and biotechnology, building a strong talent pipeline to continue advancing synthetic biology and related fields.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

2025 Society for Biological Engineering Conference Support for Future Leaders

Project Outcomes Report 
Award 2529723 

This NSF award supported registration access for trainees and early-career professionals participating in four Society for Biological Engineering conferences in 2025:

  • Synthetic Biology: Engineering, Evolution and Design (SEED) Conference – June 23-26, 2025 – Houston, Texas
  • Mammalian Synthetic Biology Workshop (mSBW) – August 11-12, 2025 – Irvine, California
  • Cell Free Systems Conference – August 20-22, 2025 – Evanston, Illinois
  • International Conference on Microbiome Engineering (ICME) – December 1-3, 2025 – Belgium

Together, these conferences brought together researchers and practitioners working across biological engineering, synthetic biology, mammalian synthetic biology, cell-free systems, microbiome engineering, biomanufacturing, automation, computational biology, therapeutics, immune engineering, and related fields. The meetings provided forums for attendees to share recent technical advances, discuss emerging challenges, and build connections that can lead to future collaborations.

The major goal of the project was to make these conferences more accessible to graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, and early-career faculty at U.S.-based institutions who are at pivotal stages in their professional development. Many trainees and early-career professionals have limited funding to attend technical meetings, even though these meetings are important for presenting research, receiving feedback, learning about cutting-edge developments, and building professional networks.

NSF support helped reduce this barrier by providing registration support across the four conferences. Complimentary registration was provided for early-career faculty at all supported conferences. For the Mammalian Synthetic Biology Workshop and the Cell Free Systems Conference, funding allowed us to subsidize registration, offering lower than typical rates for all U.S.-based graduate students, postdocs, and early career faculty ($100-200 for trainees and $200-300 for early career professionals). This support helped broaden participation and allowed more people beginning their careers to engage directly with their technical communities.

The conferences included keynote talks, technical sessions, panels, poster sessions, oral presentations, networking events, and informal discussions. These activities allowed participants to exchange research findings, learn from leaders in the field, and develop new professional relationships. Supported attendees had opportunities to present their work, receive feedback from experts, meet potential collaborators and mentors, and gain visibility within their research communities.

The project also had an impact beyond the principal discipline of biological engineering. The research communities supported by these conferences connect with medicine, agriculture, energy, food systems, advanced manufacturing, materials, chemistry, computer science, and data science. By supporting participation in meetings that bring together people from many technical backgrounds, the award helped encourage interdisciplinary exchange and collaboration.

Collectively, this grant provided complimentary and discounted registrations to approximately 120 graduate students, post-docs and early career researchers across four conferences. Supported attendees represented universities from the following states:

  • California
  • Colorado
  • Connecticut
  • Delaware
  • Florida
  • Georgia
  • Illinois
  • Indiana
  • Iowa
  • Maryland
  • Massachusetts
  • Missouri
  • Ohio
  • New Jersey
  • New York
  • South Carolina
  • Tennessee
  • Texas
  • Virginia
  • Washington
  • Wisconsin
